lessons.title: The First World War: causes, course and results

objectives: Explain the long-term causes of the First World War
Describe the main groups of countries and the course in outline
Describe the results, including the League of Nations
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the dates (28 June 1914, 11 November 1918, 1919, 1920), the lists of alliances and the MAIN scheme used in the syllabus.

blocks.md: The **First World War** began in **1914** and ended in **1918**. It involved many countries in Europe and beyond and was fought in Europe, Africa, the Middle East and at sea. Millions of soldiers and civilians died. Its causes are often summarised as **MAIN**: **M**ilitarism (arms race), **A**lliances, **I**mperialism (rivalry for colonies) and **N**ationalism (extreme national pride).

blocks.caption: Alliances before the war
blocks.alt: Two columns listing the countries of the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance.

blocks.title: Alliances and immediate cause
blocks.md: Europe was divided into two groups: the **Triple Alliance** (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the **Triple Entente** (Britain, France, Russia). On **28 June 1914** the heir to the Austrian throne, **Archduke Franz Ferdinand**, was assassinated at **Sarajevo**. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; the alliances drew in Russia, Germany, France and Britain.

The war was fought as a long, hard struggle on the **Western Front** in trenches, using machine guns, artillery, poison gas, tanks, aircraft and submarines. The **Allies** (Britain, France, Russia and later Italy, the USA and others) fought the **Central Powers** (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria). The USA joined in **1917**. Africa was affected too: German colonies were attacked, and African soldiers and carriers took part.

blocks.title: Results
blocks.md: Fighting ended with an **armistice on 11 November 1918**. The **Treaty of Versailles (1919)** punished Germany: it lost territory and all its colonies, paid reparations and limited its army. The **League of Nations** was founded (in 1920) to keep peace, but it was weak. The war also destroyed empires, left deep economic damage and sowed bitterness that contributed to a second war.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The assassination was the trigger, not the only cause.
- Do not confuse the Allies with the Central Powers.
- The armistice (11 November 1918) is not the same as the Treaty of Versailles (1919).

lessons.title: The war in Kamerun and the partition of 1916

objectives: Describe the Allied attack on Kamerun
Explain how the territory was divided
Explain the mandate system and the League of Nations
Describe the consequences of the partition
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: date of Douala's fall (September 1914), end of German resistance in early 1916, the 1916 partition and approximate proportions, mandate dates (1919–1922), and the names of the military forces.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: When war began in 1914, the Allies attacked German colonies. In **Kamerun**, British, French and Belgian forces advanced from Nigeria, French Equatorial Africa and the sea. **Douala** surrendered in **September 1914**. German forces retreated inland and held out for some time; the last important German positions fell in early **1916** (including Mora in the north), and many German troops withdrew into neighbouring Spanish territory.

items.text: Britain governed its part together with Nigeria

blocks.caption: The two parts after 1916
blocks.alt: A schematic showing a large French part and a narrow British strip on the west side.

blocks.title: Partition
blocks.md: After the German defeat, Kamerun was shared between **Britain and France**. In **1916** they agreed on a dividing line: France took the larger part (roughly four-fifths) and Britain a long, narrow strip along the Nigerian border. These were later called **British Cameroons** and **French Cameroun**. Britain governed its part as two sections, **Northern** and **Southern**, together with Nigeria.

blocks.title: Mandates
blocks.md: At the end of the war the League of Nations gave Britain and France the right to govern the former German territory as **mandates** (confirmed in **1922**). A mandate was meant as a trust: the governing power had to develop the territory and report to the League. The mandates were still, in practice, colonial rule.

**Consequences.** Families and ethnic groups were split by the new border. Two different systems — British and French — developed, with different languages, laws, school systems and currencies; these differences later mattered in the independence and reunification debates. The Germans were removed; German plantations were later sold or taken over.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- The division of 1916 was a decision of Britain and France, not of the people of Kamerun.
- A mandate is not the same as a protectorate or a trusteeship, although in practice they were similar.
- Use precise language: say 'about four-fifths', not 'exactly 80 per cent', unless the source gives the figure.

blocks.title: Example 1: what happened to Kamerun
blocks.statement: Which two powers shared the former German Kamerun after 1916?
steps: The Allies had defeated Germany in Kamerun.
Britain and France divided the territory.

blocks.title: Example 2: effect of partition
blocks.statement: How did the partition affect families on the border?
steps: The new line cut through areas where people had relatives.
Different rules, languages and currencies applied on each side.
So families found it harder to travel and trade.
blocks.answer: It split communities and made contacts harder.
